passages.t: ‘In return for my love they accuse me’, and the curses of verses 6 to 19
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David” (verse 1). The prayer begins, “O God of my praise, be not silent” (verse 1).

A man is being attacked with words. “For wicked and deceitful mouths open against me; they speak against me with lying tongues” (verse 2). He has done them good, and they repay him with hate. “In return for my love they accuse me, but I am a man of prayer” (verse 4).

Then, in verses 6 to 19, come the longest curses in the Psalms. They are spoken against one man, ‘him’. “Set over him a wicked man; let an accuser stand at his right hand” (verse 6). “May his days be few; may another take his position” (verse 8). “May his children be fatherless and his wife a widow” (verse 9). The curses go on: his children begging among ruins, his goods seized, no one kind to his orphans, his family name wiped out (verses 10 to 15). The reason follows. “For he never thought to show kindness, but pursued the poor and needy and brokenhearted, even to their death” (verse 16). He loved cursing, so let cursing cling to him like a coat (verses 17 to 19).

This part ends, “May this be the LORD's reward to my accusers, to those who speak evil against me” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The whole psalm sounds like a court case. In Israel a trial was held at the city gate, and the accuser stood beside the accused. The word for ‘accuser’ in verse 6 is satan in Hebrew. Here it means a human prosecutor, as in a courtroom. The same root comes back in verses 4, 20 and 29, where the BSB says ‘accuse’ and ‘accusers’.

The law of Moses had a rule for false witnesses. If a witness lied to ruin his brother, “you must do to him as he intended to do to his brother” (Deuteronomy 19:19). The curses follow that rule of measure for measure. The man wanted ruin for others, so let ruin fall on him.

Who is speaking in verses 6 to 19? Readers have long asked this, and the Hebrew allows two answers. Notice that the enemies are ‘they’ in verses 1 to 5 and again in verse 20, but in between the curses fall on one ‘him’. Some readers think verses 6 to 19 are the enemies' words, quoting the curse they spoke against the psalmist. Some modern translations, such as the New Revised Standard Version, add ‘They say’ before verse 6 to show this. Other readers think these are the psalmist's own words against his chief accuser, since verse 20 asks that this be the LORD's reward to them. Careful readers hold each view, and these notes do not choose.
passages.later:
After Judas betrayed Jesus, Peter quoted this psalm to the other disciples. “May another take his position” (Acts 1:20) is verse 8, and Peter used it to say that someone must take Judas's place among the twelve. He also quoted Psalm 69 in the same verse.

The God of the Bible stands on the side of widows and orphans. The law said, “You must not mistreat any widow or orphan” (Exodus 22:22). A psalm calls God “A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows” (Psalm 68:5).
passages.hard:
Verse 9 is listed on the book page among the hardest lines in the Psalms. It asks that a man's children be left without a father and his wife a widow. Nothing should make that line easy to read.

The two readings above make a real difference. If verses 6 to 19 are the enemies' curse, the worst words are not the psalmist's prayer at all; they are what was said against him. If they are his own, then they are the cry of a man being hunted by liars, who hands his rage to God instead of acting on it. Even on that reading, the Bible records the prayer honestly without asking us to make it ours. The book page's part on the cursing psalms sets out four ways Christians have read such lines, and Jesus gives the way his followers are to pray for enemies: “bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you” (Luke 6:28).

No reading of this psalm makes it right to harm anyone, least of all a child or a widow.
passages.asks:
Have you been repaid evil for good? Psalm 109 shows a man who brought that wound straight to God, words and all. Anger told to God is safer than anger acted on.

And look at verse 4. Under all the accusation, he says, ‘I am a man of prayer.’ The psalm asks what you will do when others speak lies about you. It shows one answer: keep praying, and leave the judging to God.

passages.t: ‘But You, O GOD, the Lord, deal kindly with me’
passages.happening:
Now the psalm turns. “But You, O GOD, the Lord, deal kindly with me for the sake of Your name; deliver me by the goodness of Your loving devotion” (verse 21).

The man describes himself. “For I am poor and needy; my heart is wounded within me” (verse 22). He is fading like a shadow at evening (verse 23). His knees are weak from fasting, and he has grown thin (verse 24). His accusers mock him: “when they see me, they shake their heads” (verse 25).

He asks for help, and he asks that the rescue be plain to see. “Let them know that this is Your hand, that You, O LORD, have done it” (verse 27). “Though they curse, You will bless” (verse 28).

The psalm ends in thanks. He will praise God before many (verse 30), “For He stands at the right hand of the needy one, to save him from the condemners of his soul” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Look at the ‘right hand’ in this psalm. In verse 6 an accuser was to stand at a man's right hand, the place of the prosecutor. In verse 31 God stands at the right hand of the needy one. The place of the accuser has been taken by the defender. A first hearer who knew the courtroom would feel the turn.

‘For the sake of Your name’ (verse 21) means for the sake of God's own honour and character. The man does not ask on the ground of his own goodness. He asks on the ground of who God is.

He calls himself ‘poor and needy’. In verse 16 the wicked man hunted the poor and needy to their death. So the psalmist is one of the very people his enemy preyed on. Shaking the head (verse 25) was a gesture of scorn, as in Psalm 22:7.

Verse 28 is a quiet answer to all the cursing. People may curse. God's blessing outweighs it.
passages.later:
Those who passed the cross mocked Jesus in the same way: they “heaped abuse on Him, shaking their heads” (Matthew 27:39). Peter wrote that “When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate” (1 Peter 2:23).

Paul gave a rule that answers verse 28: “Bless those who persecute you. Bless and do not curse” (Romans 12:14). And he told believers to leave room for God's justice: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath” (Romans 12:19).
passages.asks:
Verse 31 is the centre of hope in this psalm. God stands beside the needy. If you are being accused, or mocked, or worn down by lies, you are not standing alone.

Notice also what the man asks for. Not first that his enemies be crushed, but that people would see God's hand at work (verse 27). The psalm moves from cursing to blessing, and from the courtroom to praise. That is the direction it asks you to take.
